q231: Step one — digital output and the resistor
q232: “An LED is like a one-way valve that lets current through in only one direction and puts almost no resistance in its way itself. That's why, if it's connected straight to a battery, the current rises sharply and it burns out within moments. A simple resistor holds back this extra current and lets the LED stay lit at the right, safe intensity.”
q233: Now light just one LED — no blinking and no complications. You'll learn how current gets from a digital pin to the LED and why the resistor is needed.

q245: Control an LED with a button
q247: “If a digital input pin isn't connected to anything, it stays in a state called floating and reads a completely random, noisy value. A pull-down resistor ties the pin to ground when the button isn't pressed so it reads zero, or conversely a pull-up holds it at the high value; the Arduino also has a built-in version of pull-up, which is turned on with INPUT_PULLUP.”
q248: Now it's time to read an input — you'll learn how to detect a button press and connect it to an output.

q254: “A potentiometer is a variable resistor with three legs; turning its knob changes the ratio of resistance on either side, and the output voltage of the middle leg rises and falls between zero and the supply voltage. The Arduino's analog-to-digital converter reads this continuous voltage and turns it into a whole number between 0 and 1023 so the program can work with it.”
q255:
With a potentiometer you read an analog value and, with PWM, turn it into a variable LED brightness.

A microcontroller's digital pin only ever has two states: either 5 volts or 0 volts; that is, it can never produce a voltage in between (like 2.5 volts). When we use PWM, the actual voltage doesn't go up and down; instead the pin switches between 5 and 0 volts on and off at a very high speed — just like an electric switch that turns on and off so fast our eyes don't notice the flicker and only see that the LED's light has dimmed!
q256: Connect the potentiometer to an analog pin (ADC).
q257: Read the `analogRead` value (on the Arduino the ADC is 10-bit; the output range is 0 to 1023).
q258: Map the value to the PWM range (0 to 255) and change the LED's brightness with analogWrite.
q259: Watch the result in the Serial Plotter.

q263: You'll learn how to control a servo motor's angle with precise PWM pulses.

q294: The ESP32 is made by Espressif; a dual-core microcontroller up to 240 MHz that has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in. It's programmed with the same Arduino code and environment, but it's faster and can connect to the internet; that's why it's widely used in IoT projects (smart home, online sensors). Just remember its logic is 3.3 volts.
q295: ESP32 — getting to know the board
q296: Brain, antenna, USB, buttons and pins
q297: “An Arduino Uno can only work with its pins; the ESP32, besides that, connects to Wi-Fi by itself and talks to your phone over Bluetooth, all on a board the size of a few coins. Before programming, it's best to know what is where on this board.”
q298:
The ESP32 is a 32-bit microcontroller that's usually sold on ready-made boards called DevKits. This board has several main parts: the ESP32 module, which is the board's brain under a metal shield, the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth antenna, a micro-USB port with a USB-to-serial converter chip, the EN and BOOT buttons, a built-in LED and two rows of pins (GPIO).

The biggest difference from the Arduino Uno: the ESP32's logic is at 3.3 volts and 5 volts damages its pins. The nice difference is that it's programmed without a separate programmer (like the ST-Link for the Blue Pill), with just a USB cable.

In the simulator below, tap each part of the board and read its explanation.

q304: The same Arduino code, just on GPIO2
q305: “The best news about the ESP32 is that if you know Arduino code, you know this too: pinMode, digitalWrite and delay are the same. You only need to know which pin the board's built-in LED sits on: on most DevKit boards, pin 2.”
q306:
On most ESP32 DevKit boards a blue LED on the board is connected to pin GPIO2. To blink it you write the same Arduino code: set the pin as an output with pinMode, turn it on with digitalWrite(2, HIGH) and wait half a second with delay(500). Unlike the LED on the Blue Pill, this LED is active-high: HIGH means on.

Note: in the simulator use the number 2 itself (the same ledPin variable in the starter code); the LED_BUILTIN constant has a different number on different boards.

In the editor below, do the same: write code that blinks the LED on GPIO2.

q312: ESP32 — turn on a light over Wi-Fi
q313: A tiny web server on the board; commands from your phone
q314: “Until now the board only ran its own commands. Now the board connects to your home Wi-Fi, starts a tiny web server on itself, and you turn the light on and off from your phone; this is what's called IoT.”
q315:
The ESP32 can behave like a tiny website. First it connects to the router with WiFi.begin("MyHome", "12345678") and waits until WiFi.status() equals WL_CONNECTED; then it gets an IP address (for example 192.168.1.50), which we print with WiFi.localIP().

Then we start a server with the WebServer library. For each address you write a function (for example handleOn) and give it to the address with server.on("/on", handleOn). When the phone (connected to the same Wi-Fi) opens the /on address, the function runs, the LED turns on, and the reply goes back with server.send(200, "text/plain", "LED ON").

Two notes: 1) server.handleClient() must be called constantly in loop(), otherwise the board doesn't listen for requests. 2) In the simulator anonymous functions (lambdas) aren't supported; write a regular function and pass its name to server.on.

The virtual router is named MyHome and its password is 12345678. After “Run”, press the /on button on the “virtual phone”. The full code is already written in the editor; read it, run it, and if you like change it in block mode (the “Wi-Fi and web server” category).
q316: The full code is already written in the editor; read it first. In `setup()` the board connects to the router with `WiFi.begin("MyHome", "12345678");` and waits with `while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) delay(500);` until the connection is complete.
q317: `Serial.println(WiFi.localIP());` prints the board's IP address; the phone has to connect to this address.
q318: The `handleOn()` function turns the light on with `digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);` and replies to the phone with `server.send(200, "text/plain", "LED ON");`; `handleOff()` is the same, with LOW and “LED OFF”.
q319: With `server.on("/on", handleOn);` and `server.on("/off", handleOff);` each address is linked to a function, and `server.begin();` starts the server.
q320: In `loop()` there's only `server.handleClient();`; without it the board doesn't listen to the phone's requests.
q321: Press “Run”, wait for the board to come online, then press /on on the “virtual phone”; the mission completes when the LED lights.
q322: The “🧩 Blocks” mode shows this same code as blocks (the “Wi-Fi and web server” category); you can change it with blocks too. If you change the function name in the “When the browser opens address …” block, it must exactly match your own function's name.
q324: The board's brain is under this metal shield: the ESP32-WROOM-32 module with a dual-core chip up to 240 MHz, about 520 kilobytes of RAM and usually 4 megabytes of flash memory for your program. The metal shield protects the chip from noise and spreads its heat.
q326: The golden zigzag traces are the board's antenna: Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz) and Bluetooth transmit and receive from here. Don't put metal, copper or wires under the antenna and don't cover it with your hand or a metal box, otherwise the signal gets weak.
q328: The micro-USB port and the USB-to-serial converter chip (usually CP2102 or CH340) next to it. It powers the board, uploads the program from the computer and returns the output of Serial.println. Unlike the Blue Pill you don't need a separate programmer; just use a cable that carries data too.
q330: EN (Enable) is the board's reset button: pressing it runs the program from the start. Like the RESET button on an Arduino.
q332: BOOT is connected to pin GPIO0. If the board doesn't enter download mode during upload and stays stuck on the Connecting… message, hold BOOT and upload again (most boards do this by themselves). After the program runs it can also be an ordinary button.
q334: The blue LED built into the board, which on most DevKit boards is connected to GPIO2. It turns on with digitalWrite(2, HIGH) and off with LOW. (Some boards don't have an LED or put it on another pin.)
q336: Two rows of pins (GPIO) on the top and bottom of the board: about 30 usable pins with PWM, ADC, I2C, SPI and touch. The logic of all pins is 3.3 volts, so don't connect 5 volts directly to them. Some pins (34 to 39) are input-only and a few pins (like 0 and 2) have a special state at power-up.
